description: Inside schools: labelling, streaming, the hidden curriculum and anti-school sub-cultures.
content_html:
What Happens Inside Schools?

Sociologists who focus on macro-level structures — class, capitalism, patriarchy — risk overlooking the daily processes within schools that shape individual outcomes. Interactionist sociologists argue that what happens in classrooms and corridors — how teachers perceive and label pupils, how pupils are grouped, how peer cultures develop — has a profound effect on achievement that cannot be explained solely by external factors such as class or home background.

Key Fact

Processes within schools affecting achievement include: streaming, setting, labelling, the self-fulfilling prophecy and the development of anti-school subcultures.

The Hidden Curriculum Revisited

Before examining labelling, it is important to be precise about the hidden curriculum. The hidden curriculum is not what appears on the timetable — that is the formal curriculum. The hidden curriculum refers to the implicit lessons schools transmit through their everyday routines and organisation: pupils learn to queue, sit in silence, accept the authority of the teacher, observe punctuality and behave in gender-appropriate ways. Bowles and Gintis (1976) linked the hidden curriculum directly to the correspondence principle: these lessons prepare working-class pupils for factory discipline and routine employment rather than critical independent thinking. In sport, boys and girls are often directed into different activities, reinforcing gendered norms of physical behaviour alongside academic learning.

Hargreaves: Labelling Deviant Pupils

David Hargreaves’s study Deviance in Classrooms (1975) examined how teachers label pupils as “deviant” within school settings. Hargreaves found that teachers rapidly formed assessments of pupils based on limited early interactions — assessments that then became stable and resistant to change. Pupils labelled as deviant or difficult tended to be placed in lower streams, received less academic encouragement and were disproportionately subject to formal discipline. Hargreaves argued that this labelling process was self-reinforcing: once a pupil was categorised as a “troublemaker”, subsequent behaviour — even relatively minor incidents — was interpreted through that lens. Hargreaves’s research is notable because it specifically focused on the school as the site of label formation, rather than locating the source of deviant identity in the pupil’s home background.

Becker and Master Status

Hargreaves’s findings connect to Howard Becker’s broader interactionist work on labelling. Becker (Outsiders, 1963) introduced the concept of master status: a label that overrides all other aspects of a person’s identity. In the school context, once a pupil is labelled as “a problem”, that label can become their master status, colouring every interaction they have with teachers. A pupil whose master status is “troublemaker” may find that even cooperative or positive behaviour is interpreted with suspicion. The self-fulfilling prophecy then follows: the pupil internalises the label and acts in ways that confirm it, transforming a teacher’s initial (possibly inaccurate) judgement into a social reality.

Stephen Ball’s study Beachside Comprehensive (1981) investigated the introduction and effects of banding in a secondary school. Ball found that the band a pupil was placed in at the start of secondary school significantly shaped their educational trajectory regardless of actual ability. Pupils in lower bands received a less academic curriculum, had lower teacher expectations placed on them, and developed more negative attitudes towards school. Ball demonstrated that banding was not a neutral administrative process — it was laden with social consequences, particularly for working-class pupils who were disproportionately placed in lower bands. The act of grouping by ability thus became a mechanism of class reproduction.

Paul Willis’s 1977 ethnographic study Learning to Labour followed twelve working-class boys (whom Willis called “the lads”) in a West Midlands comprehensive school. Willis found that “the lads” developed a counter-school culture: a system of values that actively opposed the school’s emphasis on academic work, obedience and qualifications. The lads valued masculine physical toughness, resistance to authority and the anticipation of manual labour, seeing conformist peers (“ear’oles”) as passive and weak.

Willis’s study is significant in several ways. First, it challenged Bowles and Gintis by showing that working-class pupils actively resist rather than passively absorb the hidden curriculum. Second, it revealed the paradox that this resistance — experienced by the lads as freedom — ultimately prepared them for working-class factory jobs just as effectively as conformity would have. Third, Willis drew on interactionist ideas about peer culture while grounding the analysis in a Marxist concern with class reproduction.

Key Fact

Labelling comes first: a teacher attaches a label (“troublemaker”, “high achiever”) to a pupil. The self-fulfilling prophecy describes what happens next: the pupil internalises the label and begins to act in ways that confirm it. Hargreaves showed that this process is particularly powerful in schools, where early labels quickly become stable and resistant to revision.
exam_tip_html:
The 2024 examiner report identified the hidden curriculum question as one of the lowest-scoring items. The most common error was describing what schools teach (subjects on the timetable) rather than the implicit lessons transmitted alongside formal content. Always define the hidden curriculum as the informal, unwritten lessons of obedience, hierarchy, punctuality and gender norms — and link it explicitly to Bowles and Gintis’s correspondence principle for full marks.

On a 9-mark Discuss question about in-school processes, make sure you identify the perspective most closely associated with labelling — interactionism. Include Hargreaves (Deviance in Classrooms, 1975) and Ball (Beachside Comprehensive) as your named sociologists alongside Becker on master status. Then balance with Willis (Marxist concern with class reproduction through counter-school culture) and a feminist point on gendered labels and expectations. Reach a supported judgement.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The hidden curriculum transmits implicit lessons of conformity, obedience and hierarchy alongside formal subjects. Bowles and Gintis linked it to the correspondence principle; Hargreaves (Deviance in Classrooms, 1975) showed that teacher labelling of deviant pupils creates self-reinforcing categories that shape pupils’ trajectories.
  • Becker’s concept of master status explains how a single label can dominate all a pupil’s interactions, producing the self-fulfilling prophecy. Ball’s Beachside Comprehensive research demonstrated that banding concentrates these effects, disproportionately disadvantaging working-class pupils.
  • Willis’s Learning to Labour (1977) showed that “the lads’” counter-school culture actively resisted school authority — challenging Bowles and Gintis’s passive socialisation model — but paradoxically reproduced their class position by preparing them for manual work.

practice_questions.text:
Which sociologist studied labelling of deviant pupils in classrooms in the study 'Deviance in Classrooms' (1975)?
A) Becker
B) Ball
C) Willis
D) Hargreaves
Define the term 'self-fulfilling prophecy' in the context of education.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that the self-fulfilling prophecy involves a label causing changes in behaviour; 1 mark for explaining that this confirms the original prediction and distinguishing it from labelling itself. Example: 'The self-fulfilling prophecy is the process by which a label attached to a pupil — such as being told they are low ability — causes that pupil to behave in ways that confirm the label, so that the original prediction comes true, regardless of whether it was accurate at the start.'

practice_questions.text: Identify and describe one finding from Hargreaves's study 'Deviance in Classrooms' (1975).
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a valid finding (e.g. teachers rapidly formed stable assessments of pupils as deviant based on early interactions / labelled pupils were placed in lower streams / labelled pupils received less academic encouragement / the labelling process was self-reinforcing); 2 marks for a developed description explaining its significance. Example: 'Hargreaves found that teachers formed assessments of pupils as deviant based on limited early interactions, and these assessments became stable and resistant to change. Pupils labelled as troublemakers were then treated differently — placed in lower streams and subject to more discipline — regardless of their subsequent behaviour. Hargreaves located the source of deviant identity in the school itself rather than in the pupil's home background, a significant challenge to deficit explanations of underachievement.'

practice_questions.text: Describe what the hidden curriculum is and give two examples of what it teaches pupils.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks for two developed points. Point 1: The hidden curriculum refers to the informal, unwritten lessons transmitted by schools alongside the formal timetable. Unlike the explicit curriculum (subjects and assessment), it is not deliberately taught but is transmitted through everyday school routines and organisation. Point 2: Examples include: pupils learn obedience to authority (sitting quietly, raising their hand, not questioning the teacher); they learn punctuality (being on time is enforced, lateness is punished); they learn to accept hierarchy (teacher above pupil, head teacher above teacher); they learn gendered behaviour (PE activities, seating arrangements). Bowles and Gintis argued these lessons correspond exactly to the discipline required in the capitalist workplace. Each point needs a named example and an explanation to earn full marks.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the view that what happens inside schools is more important than home background in explaining differences in educational achievement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (8-9): Arguments supporting the view: interactionists argue that labelling by teachers (Hargreaves's deviant labelling, Becker's master status) and structural processes inside schools (Ball's Beachside — banding reflects and reinforces class) shape outcomes independently of home background; Willis shows counter-school culture is generated within the school context. Arguments against: Marxists argue in-school processes reflect wider class structures that originate outside school (Bowles and Gintis's correspondence principle is rooted in capitalism, not the classroom); Halsey shows class barriers exist before secondary school banding takes effect. At least two perspectives with named sociologists developed in detail. Sustained sociological vocabulary. Supported judgement weighing in-school versus out-of-school factors. Secure (5-7): Both sides covered, named sociologists, judgement present. Developing (3-4): One-sided or limited, some named theorists, assertive conclusion. Emerging (1-2): Basic description, little evaluation.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the usefulness of the interactionist perspective in explaining educational inequality.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10-12): Full range of arguments for and against. Arguments for interactionism: labelling theory (Hargreaves's Deviance in Classrooms; Becker's master status) explains how classroom processes produce unequal outcomes; Ball's Beachside shows banding as a micro-level mechanism of class reproduction; Willis's ethnography reveals how peer cultures develop inside schools. Arguments against: interactionism ignores macro-level causes — Bowles and Gintis (Marxist) argue inequality is rooted in capitalism, not teacher labels; Halsey shows class affects outcomes even before secondary school labelling can take effect; feminists argue patriarchal structures outside schools (Becky Francis) shape what happens inside them. A judgement that weighs whether interactionism is useful as a partial explanation, even if it does not capture the full picture of structural inequality. Comparison and contrast of perspectives is explicit. Secure (7-9): Most arguments present, named sociologists, clear judgement. Developing (4-6): Relevant but one-sided, some named theorists, assertive conclusion. Emerging (1-3): Basic description, few named sociologists, little evaluation.

knowledge_checks.q: In Willis's 'Learning to Labour' (1977), what term did Willis use for the working-class boys who actively rejected school values?
Which sociological perspective is most closely associated with labelling theory and the self-fulfilling prophecy in schools?
Ball's study of a comprehensive school investigating the effects of banding on pupils' trajectories was called '______ Comprehensive'.
Hargreaves's 1975 study, which examined how teachers label pupils as troublemakers in school, was titled 'Deviance in ______'.
Match each sociologist or concept to its correct description.
right: Showed teachers form stable deviant labels based on early classroom interactions
Found that banding at Beachside disadvantaged working-class pupils and lowered teacher expectations
Documented 'the lads' counter-school culture and its paradoxical role in class reproduction
A label that overrides all other aspects of identity, colouring all subsequent interactions

flashcard_questions.a: Placing pupils in a fixed ability group for all subjects based on an overall assessment of academic ability.
Teachers attaching definitions such as 'bright' or 'disruptive' to pupils, shaping how they are treated and how they see themselves.
A label causes a pupil to behave in ways that confirm it, making the original prediction come true.
A label that overrides all other aspects of a person's identity, defining how others see them in all interactions (Becker).

flashcard_questions.q: What did Hargreaves find in 'Deviance in Classrooms' (1975)?
flashcard_questions.a: Teachers rapidly formed stable deviant labels for pupils based on early interactions, shaping their trajectories through lower streams and reduced expectations.
Implicit lessons of obedience, hierarchy and gender norms transmitted by schools alongside formal timetabled subjects.
A peer group culture within a school that actively rejects the school's academic values, rules and goals (Willis, 1977).

flashcard_questions.q: What did Ball find in his 'Beachside Comprehensive' study?
flashcard_questions.a: Band placement shaped pupils' curriculum and teacher expectations; working-class pupils were disproportionately in lower bands.

flashcard_questions.q: How did Willis challenge Bowles and Gintis?
flashcard_questions.a: He showed pupils actively resist school rather than passively absorbing the hidden curriculum, though their resistance ironically reproduces class inequality.
A broad ability grouping system at secondary school, typically set at the start of Year 7, placing pupils in wide attainment tiers.

glossary_terms.definition: The process by which teachers and others attach definitions or categories to pupils, shaping how those pupils are treated and how they come to see themselves.
The process by which a label attached to an individual causes them to behave in ways that confirm the label, making the original prediction come true.
A label that overrides all other aspects of a person's identity, becoming the primary way they are defined by others in all interactions.
A peer group culture within a school that actively rejects the school's values, rules and academic goals, developing an alternative value system (Willis, 1977).
The informal, unwritten lessons schools transmit alongside formal subjects, including obedience to authority, punctuality and acceptance of hierarchy.
A system of broad ability grouping at secondary school, in which pupils are placed in wide attainment tiers that shape their curriculum and teacher expectations.
The allocation of pupils to fixed ability groups for all subjects, usually based on an overall assessment of academic ability at the start of secondary school.
A group of pupils within a school who share values and behaviours opposing the school's academic goals and authority structures.

hero_image_caption: Labelling and peer culture shape individual trajectories inside schools in ways that macro perspectives can overlook.
